concept: Given a sorted array of integers and a target value, find two numbers in the array that add up to the target. Return their 1-indexed positions. There is exactly one solution, and you may not use the same element twice.

solutions.label: Brute Force with Nested Loops
solutions.summary: Check every pair of elements using two nested loops to find the pair that adds up to the target.

solutions.label: Hash Map Lookup
solutions.summary: Use a hash map to store each number's index, then for each element check if its complement exists in the map.

solutions.label: Two Pointers from Both Ends
solutions.summary: Place one pointer at the start and one at the end. Move them inward based on whether the current sum is too small or too large.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Sorted Array: [2, 7, 11, 15]"] --> B["Target: 9"]
    B --> C{"Which two numbers add up to 9?"}
    C --> D["2 + 7 = 9"]
    D --> E["Return positions: [1, 2]"]
    style A fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style B fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style D fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style E fill:#f87171,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given an array of integers that is already sorted in non-decreasing order. You also receive a target number. Your task is to find two distinct elements in the array that add up to the target, and return their positions using 1-based indexing.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So the array is already sorted, and I need to return 1-indexed positions, not zero-indexed. A couple of questions: is there always exactly one valid pair, and can the array contain negative numbers or duplicates?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, there is guaranteed to be exactly one solution. The array can contain negative numbers and duplicates, but you cannot use the same element at the same index twice. The array length is at least two.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So for example, given the sorted array [2, 7, 11, 15] with a target of 9, the answer would be [1, 2] because 2 plus 7 equals 9, and those are at positions 1 and 2. Let me think about how to approach this.

sections.title: Brute Force with Nested Loops
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Array: [2, 7, 11, 15] Target: 9"] --> B["i=0, j=1: 2+7=9 ✓"]
    A --> C["i=0, j=2: 2+11=13 ✗"]
    A --> D["i=0, j=3: 2+15=17 ✗"]
    A --> E["i=1, j=2: 7+11=18 ✗"]
    A --> F["...more pairs"]
    B --> G["Found! Return [1, 2]"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style G fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#dbeafe
    style D fill:#dbeafe
    style E fill:#dbeafe

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Off the top of my head, the simplest approach is brute force. I use two nested loops. The outer loop picks each element, and the inner loop checks every element after it. If any pair adds up to the target, I return their 1-indexed positions.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can you walk through our example with that approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Sure. With [2, 7, 11, 15] and target 9, I start with i at index 0 and j at index 1. I check 2 plus 7, which is 9. That matches the target right away, so I return [1, 2]. In the worst case, though, I'd check every pair.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: It's O of n-squared because of the two nested loops, and O of 1 space since I only use a couple of index variables. This doesn't take advantage of the sorted order at all, so we can definitely do better.

sections.title: Hash Map Lookup
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Array: [2, 7, 11, 15] Target: 9"] --> B["Step 1: Visit 2"]
    B --> C["Need 9-2=7, not in map"]
    C --> D["Store 2 → index 1"]
    D --> E["Step 2: Visit 7"]
    E --> F["Need 9-7=2, found in map at index 1!"]
    F --> G["Return [1, 2]"]
    style A fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style E fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style F fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style G fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: A better approach uses a hash map. For each element, I calculate the complement, which is the target minus the current number. If that complement is already in the map, I've found my pair. Otherwise, I store the current number and its index in the map.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Walking through our example: I visit 2 first, compute 9 minus 2 equals 7. The map is empty, so I store 2 with index 1. Next I visit 7, compute 9 minus 7 equals 2. The number 2 is already in the map at index 1, so I return [1, 2].

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: That's much faster. What about the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Time is O of n since I traverse the array once. Space is O of n for the hash map. This is fast, but it uses extra memory and still doesn't leverage the fact that the array is sorted.

sections.title: Two Pointers from Both Ends
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Array: [2, 7, 11, 15] Target: 9"] --> B["left=0, right=3"]
    B --> C["2 + 15 = 17 > 9"]
    C --> D["Move right pointer left"]
    D --> E["left=0, right=2"]
    E --> F["2 + 11 = 13 > 9"]
    F --> G["Move right pointer left"]
    G --> H["left=0, right=1"]
    H --> I["2 + 7 = 9 = Target ✓"]
    I --> J["Return [1, 2]"]
    style A fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style C fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style F fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style I fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style J fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The optimal approach uses two pointers. I place a left pointer at the beginning and a right pointer at the end of the sorted array. I compute their sum. If the sum equals the target, I return those positions. If the sum is too small, I move the left pointer right to increase it. If it's too large, I move the right pointer left to decrease it.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through the example with this technique.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: With [2, 7, 11, 15] and target 9: left is at index 0, right at index 3. The sum is 2 plus 15, which is 17. That's too large, so I move right to index 2. Now the sum is 2 plus 11, which is 13, still too large. I move right to index 1. The sum is 2 plus 7, which equals 9. I return [1, 2].

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Why does this work correctly on a sorted array?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Because the array is sorted, moving left increases the sum and moving right decreases it. Each step eliminates either the largest or smallest remaining candidate, so we never skip the answer. Time is O of n and space is O of 1. It's the best we can achieve for this problem.

sections.title: Summary and Comparison
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    subgraph Comparison
        A["Brute Force\nO of n-squared time\nO of 1 space"] --> B["Hash Map\nO of n time\nO of n space"]
        B --> C["Two Pointers\nO of n time\nO of 1 space"]
    end
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great job. Can you summarize the trade-offs between the three approaches?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Brute force is O of n-squared time with constant space. The hash map improves time to O of n but costs O of n space. The two-pointer approach is the best overall: O of n time and O of 1 space, and it directly exploits the sorted property of the input. In an interview, I'd go straight to two pointers for this problem.
